lesson.title: Keep it running and secure
lesson.subtitle: Upkeep, a heartbeat, security habits and a good handover

video.title: Keep it running and secure
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph — computer studies teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph in the school garden after the holidays, holding a phone that shows 40%. Behind him, wilted seedlings.
scenes.animation: The phone's number stays frozen as the calendar flips; the seedlings droop.
scenes.narration: Over the holidays, our garden sensor said the soil was fine. Every day, the same number: forty percent. We came back to dead seedlings. The battery had died on day three, and the screen kept its last reading.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: keep a sensor project running and secure, long after launch day.

scenes.visual: A maintenance rota on the staffroom wall: a battery, a cloth, a reference thermometer, with dates and pupils' initials.
scenes.animation: Each task ticks off on the rota.
scenes.narration: Every sensor system needs upkeep, so plan it before launch. Change batteries on a schedule. Clean off dust, mud and leaves, which give false readings. And check against a trusted sensor each term, because sensors drift.

scenes.visual: A sensor sends a small pulse every hour along a line to a phone; then the pulses stop and the phone buzzes.
scenes.animation: Pulses travel along the line; a gap appears; a warning badge pops on the phone.
scenes.narration: Now the silent failure. A heartbeat is a short message a device sends on a schedule, even when nothing has changed. If the heartbeats stop, the system warns someone. No heartbeat for two hours? Check the battery, the wires and the signal.

scenes.visual: Two dashboard tiles side by side: one shows only 40%; the other shows 40% with a grey 'last seen 3 days ago' under it.
scenes.animation: The second tile's time line turns red.
scenes.narration: Show when each reading arrived, not just the number. Forty percent, last seen three days ago, tells the truth. Forty percent on its own hides the problem.

scenes.visual: Amina looks at a phone showing a tank icon at 50%, with four days ticked off on a calendar beside it. Two answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Our dashboard says the tank is half full, and it has said so for four days. What should we check first?

scenes.visual: The phone's tile flips to show 'last seen 4 days ago' in red; a heartbeat line goes flat.
scenes.animation: The time line turns red; the heartbeat flattens.
scenes.narration: Check when the last reading came. A school tank is used every day, so a number that never moves is suspicious. A heartbeat and a last-seen time would have warned you on day one.

scenes.visual: A world map dotted with cameras and routers that turn red one by one; a short list of passwords like admin and 1234 scrolls past.
scenes.animation: Red dots spread; a website card goes grey.
scenes.narration: Now security. In twenty sixteen, the Mirai malware took over hundreds of thousands of cameras and routers. It simply tried a list of about sixty factory passwords. Then it used those devices to knock major websites offline.

scenes.visual: Four padlocks click shut one after another beside a sensor box and a router.
scenes.animation: Each padlock clicks as its habit is said.
scenes.narration: So, four habits from day one. Change every default password. Install updates for the devices and the router. Put sensors on their own network, apart from school records. And collect only the data you need.

scenes.visual: A laminated one-page guide taped inside the sensor box's cabinet; a sealed envelope handed to the head teacher; two pupils learning beside an older one.
scenes.animation: Items pass from hand to hand.
scenes.narration: Projects often die when their champion leaves. So hand over early: a one-page guide by the device, and the passwords kept by the school, not on your phone. Train two people, not one. Each year, older pupils train the next class.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah beside a teacher carrying a box out of a classroom; the sensor on the wall blinks green. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. The project teacher is moving schools. The sensors work well, and only she knows the passwords. Will the system keep running?

scenes.visual: Four icons line up: a calendar, a heartbeat, a padlock, two hands passing a key.
scenes.narration: Not for long: with no guide and one person, the first flat battery ends it. Remember: upkeep on a rota, a heartbeat for silent failures, four security habits, and a handover before anyone leaves.

scenes.visual: Pupils at the board with two columns, 'how we'd notice' and 'who fixes it', filling in sticky notes.
scenes.animation: Sticky notes land in the columns.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: a failure hunt. Pupils list what could stop your sensor: a flat battery, mud, theft, a lost password, the holidays. For each: how would you notice, and who fixes it? Next time: using the data fairly.

checkpoints.prompt: The dashboard has shown the tank half full for four days. What do you check first?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a number that never changes may come from a device that has stopped. Check when it last reported.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a tank used every day doesn't stay exactly half full. The device may have stopped: check when it last reported.

checkpoints.prompt: The project teacher is leaving. The sensors work, and only she knows the passwords. Will the system keep running?

options.text: Not for long — hand it over first

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — with one person and no guide, the first flat battery or lost password ends it. A guide, passwords with the school and two trained people keep it going.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — it works today, but with one person and no guide, the first flat battery or lost password ends it.
